# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
# Review: *Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations*

This report does what a follow-up should. It registers the mediation test before the outcomes were available, adds an independent measure of hours, reports a decline rather than burying it, and answers both earlier critiques with direct evidence. Its point about the meta-analysis lands: the four studies with long follow-up were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours, so they could not speak to decay. It also frames the Halden survivors appropriately, as "survivors twice over" and an upper bound.

There are four main issues. The decline is overstated in places. An unplanned event in the control arm has gone unanalysed even though it bears directly on the trend. The new log-based hours measure doesn't mean what the paper says it means. And "confirms" is too strong for the mediation result.

## Arithmetic

These figures check out:

- Timesheet hours: 0.966 / 0.88 gives +9.8% per hour.
- Log hours: 0.966 / 0.89 gives +8.5% per hour.
- Halden continuers: 34.9 / 40.3 is a 13.4% cut in hours, and 0.968 / 0.866 gives +11.8% per hour.
- Mediation shares: 47 + 18 + 35 = 100.

## Main problems

### 1. The decline is overstated by mixing measures

Section 3 rightly treats the timesheet comparison as the like-for-like one. That measure fell from 12.5% to 9.8%, a decline of about 22%, or roughly a fifth. But two passages compare the 9-month timesheet figure with the 24-month log figure instead:

- **Summary:** "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months". That is a 32% decline, closer to a third.
- **Section 5:** "declined by about a quarter". This matches neither comparison.

The Summary and Section 5 should use 12.5% to 9.8%. The log figure can be reported separately as a 24-month level.

The decline itself is also not tested. The two confidence intervals (+6.9 to +18.4 and +4.6 to +15.2) overlap heavily. The data are consistent with fading, but they can't distinguish it from no change. Report a test of the 9-month versus 24-month difference, with its interval.

### 2. The control-arm meeting audit is contamination, and it may account for part of the decline

The month-15 meeting audit is presented as an interesting aside. In fact it changed the control condition. Two of the seven control offices raised their output per hour by 4.1% from month 15 onward. That raises the control mean, which pushes the difference-in-differences estimate down over months 15–24.

A rough calculation shows the size of the effect:

- 2 of 7 offices × 4.1% ≈ a 1.2-point rise in the control mean.
- That is close to half of the 2.7-point decline on the timesheet measure.

It may even be spillover. Control staff knew the trial was running and could see the treated offices cutting meetings. Needed:

- a sensitivity analysis excluding those two offices, or truncating at month 15;
- the treatment effect plotted month by month, so any break at month 15 is visible.

This matters for the novelty question. Some of the apparent fading may be the control group improving, not the treated group declining.

The control meeting figures also need checking. If two offices are at 5.0 hours and the control mean is 7.0, the other five must average about 7.8, up from roughly 7.2. That may be correct, but it should be reported explicitly. Otherwise state which period the 7.0 refers to.

### 3. Log-in time measures time on cases, not total working time

Active time on the case-management system captures time spent working on cases. It does not capture meetings, email, phone calls or other non-system work. So it is not a "stricter" measure of total hours, and it can't settle whether timesheets understate total work.

That changes how the log results should be read:

- **The 11% and 12% figures measure different things.** Log time falling 11% against timesheets falling 12% is what you'd expect if meeting time was cut and time on cases was protected. It isn't evidence of "slightly more work than timesheets".
- **Output per log hour is productivity per hour spent on cases.** That is a useful quantity, but a different one from output per hour worked.
- **This changes what the mediation result means.** Meeting time isn't in the denominator of the outcome. So if meetings explain 47% of the gain in output per *case* hour, fewer meetings must be making time on cases itself more efficient, for example through fewer interruptions or longer focused blocks. That is a different mechanism from "removing low-value time" from the working week. It is arguably the more interesting finding, but the paper should say which one it is claiming.

Needed: the level of log hours, not just the change, at baseline and at 24 months. Also a definition of "active", for instance whether idle sessions time out.

### 4. "Confirms" is too strong for the mediation result

Registering the analysis before the outcomes were available was the right step. Four limits remain.

- **It isn't independent replication.** The hypothesis came from the 9-month data on these same seven treated offices. Registration guards against analytic flexibility, but it doesn't make this an out-of-sample test.
- **The effective sample is still 14 offices.** Office-months are not independent. If the confidence intervals treat them as if they were, the 28–66% interval for meetings is too narrow.
- **Meeting cuts weren't randomised.** Treatment was randomised, but how much each office cut its meetings was not. Offices with more capable managers may have cut more meetings and also improved in other ways. The Limitations section mentions the no-unmeasured-confounding assumption, but the Summary's "confirms" ignores it.
- **The fatigue pathway is marginal.** Its interval (2 to 34%) barely excludes zero. The unexplained share should also be reported with an interval.

"Supports" would be accurate. "Confirms" is not.

### 5. Inference with few clusters is still unaddressed

The trial has seven offices per arm, and every estimate in Table 1 and Table 2 depends on cluster-level inference. As noted for the 9-month report, conventional cluster-robust standard errors understate uncertainty with this few clusters. Randomisation inference or a wild cluster bootstrap should be reported for at least the main per-hour estimate and the mediation shares.

The paper's claim that the 8.5% gain "excludes zero by a clear margin" may survive the correction. But it needs to be shown, not assumed.

### 6. Backlogs are still missing

The 9-month report flagged backlogs building beyond statutory deadlines as a specific risk to check at follow-up. At 24 months the paper still reports no measures of backlog size, time to decision, or the share of cases closed near the deadline. A stable count of cases closed can hide a growing queue, so these should be in Table 1.

## Halden subset

- **Non-response.** Only 14 of the 23 organisations responded. The nine that didn't may include more reversions, and if so, 3 of 14 understates the true reversion rate. The paper should say what is known about the nine, even if only their sector and continuation status.
- **The "client-facing" label is applied after the fact.** The marketing agency reverted because of client deadlines, which most discretionary work also has. Folding it into "client-facing or coverage obligations" stretches the work-type distinction. It's more honest to report it as a reversion in a discretionary-sector organisation.
- **Baseline hours.** The 40.3-hour baseline matches the 27-organisation time-tracking group in Varga & Holm, but the 11 continuers are a different subset. Confirm that 40.3 is this subset's own baseline.
- **Survivors show no decay.** The corrected Halden subset was at 10.8% at 6 months and the 11 continuers are at 11.8% at 24 months. That contrasts with Varden's decline, and it is what survivor selection would predict. Stating this contrast explicitly would strengthen the paper's own "upper bound" framing.
- **Halden's attrition is still unexplained.** Varga & Holm reported that seven of the nine withdrawals happened after the reduced schedule began, contrary to the working paper's account. With a Halden author on this report, it is a natural place to acknowledge or correct that.

## Smaller points

- **Counter-arm cost.** Restoring service with 12% more staff at full pay suggests roughly a 12% rise in staff cost per contact. The 9% figure presumably reflects non-staff costs or some recovery in contacts handled. Say which.
- **Sick days.** The 27% fall still doesn't account for the shorter schedule mechanically reducing the days on which sickness can be recorded. Report it per scheduled day.
- **Resignations.** These have no confidence intervals and are not shown as a difference-in-differences against baseline.
- **Timing of the follow-up protocol.** It was registered at month 11, after the 9-month results were public. That is fine, and it is disclosed, but it should be acknowledged as a point against independence (see problem 4).
- **Response to Varga & Holm.** "Not supported" is fair. Their prediction that the gain would fall to zero by month ten was based on extrapolating self-reported energy in a different population. So the Varden result refutes their conclusion rather than testing their model. The current wording is close to this; it just shouldn't go further.

## Overall

The report substantially advances the debate. A per-hour gain of roughly 8–10% persists at two years under the strongest design so far. It is smaller than at nine months, and meeting reductions plausibly account for a large share of it.

Five revisions would make it secure:

1. Use like-for-like figures for the decline and test whether it is significant.
2. Analyse the control-arm meeting audit as contamination.
3. Reinterpret log hours as time spent on cases, and follow through on what that means for the mediation result.
4. Change "confirms" to "supports" and use inference suited to 14 clusters.
5. Report backlog measures.

The meeting audit points to the natural next study: a trial with an arm that reorganises work without reducing hours. That is the only design that can show whether the hours cut is the cause or the catalyst.

I can sketch that three-arm design, or draft a corrected Summary.
